title: Thailand Scraps 60-Day Visa-Free Entry for Over 90 Nations — What Indian Travellers Need to Know
excerpt: A sweeping policy reversal cuts visa-free stays from 60 to 30 days and restricts land-border entries, as Bangkok pivots from tourism promotion to a security-first approach that will reshape how NRIs plan their favourite Southeast Asian getaway.
body:
For the better part of two years, Thailand extended an unusually generous welcome mat. In July 2024, visitors from more than 90 countries — India included — could enter the kingdom without a visa and stay for up to 60 days, double the earlier limit. It was part of a post-pandemic push to revive a tourism sector that accounts for more than a tenth of GDP. Last week, the Thai cabinet voted to take that mat back.

Under the revised framework approved on Tuesday, most visa-free stays will be capped at 30 days. Citizens of certain countries — yet to be announced — may be limited to just 15 days. Travellers using the 30-day scheme will also face a cap of two visa-free land-border entries per calendar year, a measure aimed at ending the "border-run" practice long favoured by long-stay visitors who hopped across a frontier and came straight back.

The government has not set an effective date for the rollback, but Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said the changes would come into force once the Visa Policy Committee finalises country-by-country terms.

## Why Now? A Crackdown on "Grey-Market" Operations

The catalyst, Thai officials say, is an alarming spike in crime involving foreign nationals. In recent months, authorities have arrested foreigners linked to drug trafficking, human smuggling, sex trafficking, and the operation of unlicensed businesses including hotels and language schools. Tourism Minister Surasak Phancharoenworakul said the extended stays had been "exploited by individuals involved in grey-market businesses and online scam operations."

Government spokesperson Rachada Dhanadirek acknowledged the trade-off bluntly: "Tourists provided benefits, such as boosting the economy, but the current scheme has allowed some people to exploit it."

The Royal Thai Police have also launched a separate three-month crackdown targeting transnational crime, illegal immigration, and cybercrime involving foreign nationals, with proposals for a permanent joint task force.

## What This Means for Indian Travellers

Thailand is one of the most popular international destinations for Indian passport holders. Under the current bilateral arrangement, Indians enjoy visa-free entry for 30 days for tourism — the same duration that will become the new standard for most nationalities. In practical terms, Indian travellers may see little change to the length of their allowed stay.

But the restrictions on repeat land-border entries are significant for NRIs who use Thailand as a base for broader Southeast Asian travel, and for digital nomads who previously relied on the 60-day window — or serial re-entries — to work remotely from places like Chiang Mai or Koh Phangan.

For those seeking longer stays, Thailand's Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) remains an option. Launched in 2024, the DTV offers a five-year, multiple-entry visa for remote workers and digital nomads, with each stay extendable up to 360 days. It requires proof of 500,000 Thai Baht (roughly ₹12 lakh) in liquid funds.

## Tourism Numbers Under Pressure

The timing is delicate. Foreign arrivals to Thailand fell 3.4 per cent year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, with visitors from the Middle East plunging by nearly a third. Despite this and the tighter restrictions, Bangkok is maintaining its target of 33.5 million foreign tourists for the year — a slight bump from the nearly 33 million recorded in 2025.

The bet is that genuine, high-value travellers will keep coming regardless, while the new limits will deter those who overstay or exploit the system.

## What NRIs Should Do Now

Anyone planning a Thailand trip in the coming months should keep a few things in mind. First, 30-day visa-free entry still works fine for most holidays. Second, carry proof of a return ticket, hotel bookings, and sufficient funds — immigration officers are expected to be more vigilant. Third, if longer stays or repeated visits are on the cards, investigate the DTV or a proper tourist visa in advance rather than banking on border runs.

For the millions of Indians who flock to Bangkok, Phuket, and Pattaya each year, Thailand is not closing its doors. But it is asking visitors to knock first.
